results.title: Antino Backdoor Uses Outlook and OneDrive for C2 in China-Nexus Espionage Campaign
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Government and policy organizations across Asia have become the target of a new campaign orchestrated by a China-nexus threat actor.
The activity, which has targeted government and policy organizations in Taiwan, India, the Philippines, Cambodia, Pakistan, Thailand, and Myanmar, involves the deployment of a previously undocumented backdoor codenamed Antino. Cisco Talos is tracking the cluster under the moniker UAT-11587.
The threat actor was first detected in September 2025 in connection with a spear-phishing campaign directed against Taiwan's academic, think tank, and civil society policy community. Since then, attacks linked to the intrusion set have expanded to target 16 entities across eight Asian countries.
"Antino is a Rust-compiled Windows backdoor that supports host reconnaissance, shell and PowerShell execution, file transfer, in-memory shellcode loading and persistence," security researcher Ashley Shen said. "Its native command-and-control channel operates exclusively through Microsoft 365, using Microsoft Graph to interact with Outlook and OneDrive."
UAT-11587 is assessed to share some level of overlap with Jewelbug, which, in turn, exhibits tactical similarities with China-aligned clusters known as CL-STA-0049, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon, and REF7707. A report published by Broadcom-owned Symantec and Carbon Black in August 2026 characterized Jewelbug as a China-based hackers-for-hire group that carries out espionage operations and a for-profit cryptocurrency fraud business.
However, Cisco Talos said its own investigation has failed to unearth a connection between the espionage campaign and Jewelbug's financially motivated activity, prompting it to designate UAT-11587 as a separate activity set.
The challenges in establishing definitive links notwithstanding, the adversary has been classified as China-nexus with high confidence, citing the presence of zh-CN language and Simplified Chinese metadata in the lure documents and the UTC+08:00 time zone in the spear-phishing message header.
"The campaign's lure theme and targeting provide additional contextual support," Talos said. "Its lures and observed targets include Taiwanese political, legislative, civil defense, and policy research subjects, together with regional government, maritime, diplomatic, and security themes. This collection focus is consistent with China-nexus actor interests."
Two other indicators that point to a China-nexus are below -
- Nearly a dozen distinct Antino build outputs feature Cargo registry paths referencing rsproxy[.]cn, a high-speed domestic mirror and proxy service for crates.io catering to mainland China
- A JavaScript downloader associated with UAT-11587 that references "d32tpl7xt7175h.cloudfront[.]net," a CloudFront domain previously flagged by Arctic Wolf in connection with a campaign conducted by a China-affiliated threat actor known as UNC6384 targeting European diplomatic and government entities last year using an unpatched Windows shortcut vulnerability.
Evidence indicates that UAT-11587 has also trained its sights on organizations in Syria around May 2026, indicating a focus beyond Asia. Attacks mounted by the threat actor have been found to spike between March and early June 2026, with a "concentrated wave" taking place on June 8 and 9, 2026, targeting dozens of systems associated with government IT infrastructure.
While the choice of spear-phishing as an initial access vector is unsurprising, the choice of the lures employed suggests the threat actor conducted extensive reconnaissance of the target organizations in order to tailor the content and maximize the chance of success.
In an attempt to lend credibility to the emails, UAT-11587 is said to have spoofed sender identities trusted by the intended recipients to bypass SPF and DMARC security checks and ensure that the messages land on the victims' inboxes.
"Another social engineering technique used for initial access in this campaign was the closely replicated reconstruction of Gmail's native attachment preview widget inside the email HTML body," Shen explained. "The actor replicated the styling of Gmail's attachment card using four inline PNG images embedded as Base64-encoded MIME parts."
"The entire attachment card was wrapped in an anchor tag pointing to an attacker-controlled [Cloudflare Pages] URL. When a Gmail user opens the email in a browser, Gmail's renderer faithfully displays the attacker-controlled HTML, producing a fake attachment widget that is visually indistinguishable from a legitimate Gmail attachment preview."
An analysis of the lures demonstrates a propensity to target audiences interested in foreign affairs, international security, and government policy, Talos added. The attack chain itself is a five-stage process that begins with a HTA or WSF stager and culminates in the deployment of Antino.
The Cloudflare URL in the phishing email leads to the download of an HTA or WSF file that's then executed to retrieve a JavaScript downloader and decryptor. The next stage triggers a .NET deserialization chain to load "TestAssembly.dll," a .NET downloader and launcher that's responsible for three actions -
- Download and open the lure document to the victim.
- Download a decoy Calculator executable.
- Download and launch the Antino backdoor.
The implant ("slc.dll") is launched by means of DLL sideloading using a legitimate Microsoft-signed binary ("GatherOsState.exe"). Once launched, the Rust-compiled malware communicates with Microsoft 365 applications and uses Outlook and OneDrive objects as dead drops, instead of depending on a conspicuous dedicated command-and-control (C2) server.
Antino is no different from other backdoors of its kind in that it supports host reconnaissance, command execution, and persistence. It can also list running processes, enumerate directories, run PowerShell scripts, shellcode, operator-supplied programs, and commands using "cmd.exe"
For C2, it uses Outlook for command exchange and OneDrive for heartbeat and file transfer. Specifically, it fetches commands from the threat actor's Outlook mailbox folder every 10 seconds by looking for messages with the subject prefix "command_req_[session_id]."
"The Antino backdoor abuses the Windows Scripted Diagnostics framework to execute attacker-controlled PowerShell through legitimate Windows components," Talos said. "This can complicate behavioral attribution to the original implant, although it does not eliminate observable PowerShell, file-creation, or Registry telemetry."
results.summary:
A China-nexus threat actor identified as UAT-11587 is deploying a sophisticated Rust-based backdoor called Antino to target government and policy organizations across Asia and the Middle East.

### Key Points
- Cisco Talos identified the UAT-11587 cluster, which has compromised 16 entities across eight countries, including Taiwan, India, and the Philippines.
- The Antino backdoor uses Microsoft 365 services, specifically Outlook and OneDrive, as a command-and-control channel to evade traditional network detection.
- Attackers utilize highly tailored spear-phishing emails that spoof Gmail attachment previews to bypass security filters and deceive high-profile targets.
- The malware employs DLL sideloading via a legitimate Microsoft-signed binary, "GatherOsState.exe," to maintain persistence on infected Windows systems.
- Evidence linking the campaign to China includes Simplified Chinese metadata, specific Cargo registry paths, and targeting themes consistent with regional geopolitical interests.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights a growing trend of threat actors abusing legitimate cloud infrastructure to conduct stealthy, long-term espionage against government and diplomatic entities. By leveraging trusted platforms like Microsoft 365, attackers significantly complicate detection efforts for security teams relying on traditional traffic monitoring.

results.title: Google Workspace Weekly Recap - October 2, 2026
results.author: Paul Jiménez Vela
results.content:
October 2, 2026
Google Workspace Weekly Recap - October 2, 2026
Create more natural, expressive AI voiceovers in Google Vids with upgraded Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite TTS
We are upgrading the underlying text-to-speech (TTS) engine powering AI voiceovers and avatar narration in Google Vids to the latest Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite TTS model. | Learn more.
Introducing skills in the Gemini app and Workspace, plus what’s next for Gems
We recently introduced skills—reusable prompts that guide Gemini—in the Gemini app and Google Workspace. Over the coming weeks, skills will roll out to Workspace users and eventually replace Gems as the tool for tailoring instructions for specific tasks. | Learn more.
Customize the style of your captions in Google Vids
Captions in Google Vids are now fully customizable. Until now, captions came in a set style. You can now change their font and typography, where they sit on screen, and how they animate, so they match your brand or the look of your video. | Learn more.
Programmatic comment and suggestion support now available in the Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides APIs
Developers can now programmatically create, read, and manage comments across Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides using their respective developer APIs. In Google Docs, this update also introduces API support for suggested edits, allowing automated tools and third-party systems to propose document revisions for user review rather than altering content directly. | Learn more.
Simple setup option for Workspace Client-side encryption
We are introducing a new option which can make the initial setup of Google Workspace Client-side encryption (CSE) significantly easier and faster for admins. | Learn more.
Find your learning tools all in one place with the student hub in Gemini
We recently announced a new, dedicated hub in the Gemini app to help get students started with all of Gemini's learning tools. Initially available in personal accounts, the Gemini student hub is now available to Google Workspace for Education users of all ages. | Learn more.
Built-in interoperability between Google Meet and Microsoft Teams on Android (AOSP) devices, now generally available
We are making video conferencing device interoperability between Google Meet and Microsoft Teams generally available. It was previously available in preview. | Learn more.
The announcements above were published on the Workspace Updates blog over the last week. Please refer to the original blog posts for complete details.
results.summary:
Google has announced several updates to its Workspace platform, including the integration of Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite for voiceovers and new programmatic API support for document comments.

### Key Points
- Google Vids now features Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite for improved AI voiceovers and offers fully customizable caption fonts, positioning, and animations.
- The Gemini app is introducing "skills" to replace Gems, providing reusable prompts for task-specific guidance across Workspace applications.
- Developers can now programmatically manage comments in Docs, Sheets, and Slides, with added support for suggested edits in Google Docs.
- Google Workspace for Education users now have access to a dedicated student hub within the Gemini app for centralized learning tools.
- Interoperability between Google Meet and Microsoft Teams is now generally available for Android-based video conferencing devices.
- Administrators can utilize a new, simplified setup process for Google Workspace Client-side encryption to improve deployment speed.

### Why it Matters
These updates streamline content creation and administrative workflows while enhancing cross-platform compatibility for enterprise and educational users. By integrating advanced AI tools and improving API functionality, Google is positioning its ecosystem to better support automated document management and collaborative video conferencing.

results.title: 'Hands off our NHS data:'Inside the nationwide movement against Palantir’s £330m NHS deal
results.author: chiara.castro@futurenet.com (Chiara Castro) , Chiara Castro
results.content:
It’s 4 pm on an unusually warm first day of October as a small crowd begins forming outside the Bristol Royal Infirmary, the south-west UK city’s central hospital. Outpatients arriving for appointments begin to take notice as the demonstration against US company Palantir’s involvement with the UK’s health service starts to take shape.
Placards are raised: “No Palantir in our NHS”, “Ditch Palantir”, “Good at harvesting your NHS data”. The passing traffic starts beeping its support.
Bristol is one of the 45 locations across over 30 cities around the UK where people are taking to the streets on October 1, 2026. The biggest action rolls out in front of Palantir’s London offices, with hundreds there to protest. Here, the number is closer to a vocal 50 or so.
Former and current health workers, campaigners from Amnesty International, the Good Law Project and more, and concerned citizens have all joined the International Day against Palantir to ask the British government to stop paying a US firm to manage UK citizen health data.
Headquartered in Miami, Palantir Technologies is an analytics firm specialising in AI-powered tools designed to manage large datasets. Its flagship software platforms, Gotham and Foundry, are widely used by government organizations and businesses globally to uncover data patterns and support decision-making operations.
The promise of its products certainly makes sense. Its list of clients, however, is what today’s demonstrators find less than palatable.
Among its most controversial partners is the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, better known as ICE, which has been using Palantir tech for over a decade. More recently, the Israeli military has also begun using its powerful software to assist with on-the-ground operations.
It was in 2023 that Palantir managed to secure a £330 million contract within the UK public health sector. The then-Prime Minister, Rishi Sunak, tasked the American company with building a new platform to manage all UK citizen health data across the country in what was called the NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP).
Three years and two Prime Ministers later, the project is under increasing scrutiny, with some suggestions from insiders that many of the hospitals that have been signed up to Palantir are still yet to even log into the system.
With more than one reason for protester complaint on the table, TechRadar went along to the Bristol arm of the International Day of Action to find out what it was that the demonstrators cared about the most — their data, their finances or their politics?
Palantir’s NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP): the privacy concerns
A national programme led by NHS England, the Federated Data Platform (FDP) is designed to help NHS organisations bring together information from hundreds of different databases in a single platform. The goal is undoubtedly attractive: improve efficiency by supporting health worker delivery of patient care, improving operational performance, and assisting staff to make better-informed decisions.
According to the NHS security and privacy page, “the protection of people’s data is at the heart” of FDP’s design, with measures like strong network security, purpose-based access to data, and encryption all in place. It certainly sounds well conceived and considered.
Furthermore, under the terms of the contract with the NHS, Palantir Technologies is named strictly as a "data processor". That means it cannot decide how the information that its software processes is used. In other words, Palantir could face direct liability should it fail to secure this data or violate NHS instructions.
A Palantir spokesperson explained to TechRadar that FDP is a software that helps the NHS better manage the data it already holds. “How that software is used is controlled by the NHS Trusts who use it, with data — legally and contractually — only able to be processed strictly in accordance with their instructions, and all data remaining in the UK,” they added.
Despite these rules of engagement, all of the protesters expressed their lack of trust in Palantir when it came to handling their most sensitive data. They were not convinced that Palantir was not able to access their information at will.
“We simply cannot believe this won’t happen,” one protester told us.
These concerns do not exist in a vacuum. In May, the Financial Times reported on an internal NHS briefing note which explicitly earmarked "unlimited access" to identifiable patient data for certain contractor admin roles.
Most protesters also expressed their fear that Palantir’s NHS system could also be repurposed one day for wider surveillance across different government bodies, such as immigration.
Matt, a health worker and campaigner in Bristol, told TechRadar that there’s both an emotional and technical component to his worries about Palantir.
“All Palantir software is interoperable with each other. So, the data that is collected under the FDP can be dragged and dropped to their policing software if a government chose to do that,” he said.
Matt refers to what came out of a January investigation by The Nerve that found 34 active contracts across at least 10 UK government departments, as well as local councils and police authorities. A scenario that, according to opponents, could make it technically easier for a cross-pollination of healthcare data and law enforcement work to occur.
Again, these fears aren’t entirely unfounded. While Palantir’s UK CEO, Louis Mosley, insists that Palantir has “no interest” in UK patient data, the company’s track record outside the country seems to tell a different story.
404Media revealed that, in the US, citizen health data is fed to a Palantir-developed app called ELITE, which is used by ICE agents to map and target suspected illegal immigrants.
Small wonder, then, why Matt and others outside the Bristol Royal Infirmary are expressing their concerns.
Is Palantir’s technology worth the risk?
Make no mistake, though. This was mostly a protest of politics rather than privacy. Most people at the rally were here to object to Palantir's deal with the NHS based on the company’s involvement in ongoing global conflicts and immigration raids.
Either way, though, as the Head of Tech and Data at Good Law Project (one of the campaigns behind the UK actions), Duncan McCann, told TechRadar, procurement decisions based on ethics and morals are rare, whatever field of concern they lie in. The hard facts of cost and utility most usually win the day.
And it's because of this, McCann explains, that the tide is turning against the US firm.
“When we started working on this campaign a year ago, all the momentum was with Palantir. They were getting new contracts all the time. The assumption was that this contract was just going to get renewed. It wasn't even really a question. Now, when I look around, I see them losing contracts,” said McCann, mentioning the Homes for Ukraine as the most telling example.
And, for McCann, the reason for Palantir’s decline is simpler than the politics. Its technology isn’t just more expensive — Ukraine said the government saved millions by replacing Palantir’s software — but it seems to be actually failing in its goal of making the NHS more efficient.

While the UK government claims to have already seen significant improvements in its data management flow, there have been multiple reports alleging that the FDP software is not delivering on that promise.
A report by Democracy for Sale, for example, says that staff have found that Palantir's newly built platform is 10 times slower than the existing system, citing an internal NHS document.
Palantir has strongly rejected these allegations, however. In a statement to Democracy for Sale, the US firm argued that "comparing the two systems is not like-for-like", adding that its platform "introduces guardrails to improve data correctness, enforce purpose-based access and allow more controlled data sharing".
Approached by TechRadar, a Palantir spokesperson said:
“Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with Trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3 per cent reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6 per cent improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”
Impressive-sounding stats, but back in June 2026, the Financial Times reported that England’s health service acknowledged that its main claims about the benefits of the FDP aren’t backed up by robust evidence, with MPs now calling for a new audit.
The jury, it seems, is still out on the Palantir systems’ efficacy, leaving the company’s reputation a peg or two lower than where it stood when the 2023 UK government originally signed the deal.
How likely is it for Burnham to scrap the deal?
As the deadline to renew the deal approaches, campaigners feel that now is their best shot at making the government listen to their concerns. Indeed, this may be more likely than some people realise, given the new Prime Minister’s position on digital policy.
During Andy Burnham’s almost decade as Mayor of Greater Manchester, neither municipal nor public health departments awarded any contracts to Palantir. Instead, Manchester’s NHS leaders spent six years building their own analytics infrastructure.
For campaigners against Palantir’s involvement in the NHS, then, scrapping the deal could be a good fit for Burnham’s political agenda.
"It proves that we can do it ourselves and save money by doing that, while creating new jobs,” McCann from the Good Law Project told TechRadar.
What’s certain is that the new Prime Minister is under increasing political pressure to act.
During this week's Labour Party conference, 20,000 party members backed a motion to cancel the contract with the US firm. Although the motion was not chosen for debate, the number of signatories still signals the discontent among the political rows.
A great majority of Labour voters (76%) also believe Palantir’s contract should not be renewed when it expires in February 2027. That echoes the views of the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee that, in June, urged the government to exercise the 2027 break clause and “either develop an in-house replacement or seek an alternative UK provider”.
That said, as Wired reported, there are plenty of politicians and advisers close to Burnham who are also quietly advocating for the company’s work in the UK. The recent announcement that former Labour Deputy Leader, Tom Watson, is joining Palantir as senior vice president perfectly paints the rifts within the governing Party.
For the people filling the streets, however, it isn’t negotiable. Ultimately, as health worker and campaigner Matt points out, the change could, and should, start locally.
"Here, in Bristol," he says, "we're really trying to build up the pressure and give the message that NHS Trusts actually do have the right to refuse to use the software. We really want them to take a strong stance on that."
What are the Palantir protesters asking for
By Wednesday, September 30, the day before the demonstrations, 44,000 people had filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in, or used by the FDP system operated using the US company’s AI technology. Thousands of people have also signed petitions to ask to scrap the £330 million deal in the past months.
Currently, patients cannot opt out of having their sensitive healthcare data stored on the FDP, despite a 2023 YouGov poll finding that nearly half of all UK adults would likely opt out of data sharing if a private company like Palantir began processing their personal information.
“I think when people are aware of it, they're very concerned,” health worker Matt told TechRadar, pointing out the number of people turning up to the rally. “It really shows the strength of the public feeling about this.”
The erosion of trust in the NHS was a recurrent topic when we spoke to those opposing Palantir in Bristol. Many told TechRadar that they would opt out if they could.
And while people admitted that a better system to manage health data may be needed, they didn’t feel that Palantir should be the answer.
“We do need platforms that can speak to each other, but we need ones that we can trust,” another protester told us.
Most people said that they would feel more comfortable if a UK company managed their data instead. They said a domestic firm would be easier to oversee and hold to account.
Economics was also a big concern.
"Why can't these jobs be kept in Britain for British companies to run these systems? Why do we need to have a foreign company coming in and have dangerous motives to actually do this work? It's not necessary," another protester told us.
As we left the rally, the placards still waiving in the distance and the hospital entrance regaining its usual look, it was that word 'trust' that echoed in our mind.
It's almost impossible to separate the issues of data privacy from global politics, when it comes to Palantir. It's tangled up in every line of code.
Demonstrators in Bristol weren't rallying around a single, isolated grievance. They were there to resist a model where healthcare, data, and defense contracts bleed into one another.
At its very core, the entire issue around people’s health data privacy hinges on public trust.
Whether driven by fear of corporate overreach, frustration at the use of government funds, or deeper ethical objections, the battle over Palantir goes beyond digital security – the public is demanding assurances about who holds their most sensitive information.
And, for those taking to the streets today, the US tech giant had failed to earn their trust.

results.summary:
Protesters across the UK held demonstrations on October 1, 2026, demanding the government terminate its £330 million contract with Palantir Technologies for managing sensitive NHS patient health data.

### Key Points
- Demonstrations occurred in over 30 UK cities, including London and Bristol, to oppose Palantir’s role in the NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP).
- Critics cite concerns over Palantir’s history with US immigration enforcement and military operations, fearing potential misuse of UK health data.
- The £330 million FDP contract, awarded in 2023, faces scrutiny over claims of poor system performance and lack of transparent evidence regarding efficiency gains.
- Over 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their data being processed by the platform, which currently lacks an opt-out mechanism for patients.
- Political pressure is mounting as 76% of Labour voters and various parliamentary committees urge the government to utilize a 2027 break clause.

### Why it Matters
The controversy highlights a growing public conflict between the need for modernized digital healthcare infrastructure and the demand for data sovereignty and ethical corporate partnerships. As the government weighs the contract's renewal, the outcome will set a significant precedent for how the UK manages public trust and private sector involvement in sensitive national services.

results.title: This Shoe Company’s Instagram Ad With a Frat Is Pissing People Off
results.author: Ej Dickson
results.content:
A popular national footwear brand recently published a collaborative Instagram post with a fraternity, despite two former members being recently accused of disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a fellow college student.
On September 25, HeyDude, a viral shoe brand that was acquired by Crocs in 2022, posted a photo on its Instagram account promoting shoes that appeared to be UF versions of the brand’s popular “Wally” loafer, a lightweight slip-on sneaker with a foam insert.
“@heydude called, @thetachiflorida answered,” the caption read, alongside photos of Theta Chi members clowning around and wearing orange-and-blue sneakers. The brand also posted a video on its TikTok account outside of the Florida fraternity house with the caption “wtf is any shoe besides a HEYDUDE?”
The post led to backlash in the comments section, with many questioning why the brand would choose to work with the fraternity. “#CancelHeyDude,” one person wrote. Another chimed in: “I would boycott if I wore fucking ugly shoes but I don’t so I can’t.”
As WIRED previously reported, two former members of the UF chapter of Theta Chi, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, allegedly used anonymous burner accounts with the handles "Steve 'SC’ Cumfull" and "Arnie_Grape16" to disseminate a nonconsensual intimate video of Maddie Kowalski, then a 19-year-old UF student. One of the "Steve 'SC' Cumfull" posts on X identified Kowalski by her full name and sorority affiliation.
According to affidavits from the Gainesville Police Department, the posts accumulated thousands of views. Kowalski’s name went viral on X, causing her “widespread public humiliation and significant emotional distress,” according to the affidavit. Ahmed and Pitfield are currently being charged with sexual cyberharassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine. Kowalski is also suing both men for financial damages in Florida Northern District Court. Through their attorneys, Pitfield (who has entered a plea of not guilty) and Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Though no other Theta Chi members have been charged, a screengrab of Instagram comments from an account linked to Ahmed appears to show fellow members referencing his alleged burner name. Some comments also appear to reference a cryptocurrency in Kowalski’s name, that the police affidavit alleges Ahmed promoted on X. When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer previously told WIRED that the alleged behavior described in the affidavit is “reprehensible” and “completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals.”
The charges against Pitfield and Ahmed, as well as WIRED’s reporting on the case, sparked an outcry on the UF campus. On September 15, a group of students advertised a protest outside the Theta Chi fraternity house, circulating a flier demanding that the chapter be removed from the UF campus. “They need to be held accountable,” the flier reads.
On YikYak, the anonymous campus forum, there have also been calls to “boycott” or “nuke” Theta Chi, according to screengrabs reviewed by WIRED. Some anonymous YikYak posts appeared to suggest that the September 15 protest was broken up by campus police outside of Theta Chi: “Cops nuked the theta chi protest good job UF,” one reads. “Typical.” Blake Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for UF, tells WIRED that while “there were calls and social media posts for a protest,” she was on site and “none emerged.” She clarified that, as standard UF practice, university police were present “to ensure the safety and security of all.”
Founded in 1856, Theta Chi has established more than 246 chapters at colleges and universities across the country, and it has more than 250,000 initiated members nationwide, according to the organization’s website. At UF specifically, Theta Chi has 190 active members, according to the UF Interfraternity Council.
When asked about the post with HeyDude, a representative for Theta Chi tells WIRED Ahmed and Pitfield are no longer members of Theta Chi Fraternity. “If it is determined through the legal process that the defendants are guilty of the alleged behavior described in the complaints, Theta Chi will support the maximum allowable penalty under the law and the permanent expulsion of the student offenders from the University of Florida,” the spokesperson says.
In mid-September, the Cornell Sun published the names of seven Cornell University students who a former student alleged gang-raped her in 2024 at a Chi Phi frat house; In September, the Jane Doe filed civil cases against them. The revelation has sparked widespread criticism of frat culture on social media. The content creator and activist @bluraybeyond, who has also posted about the Kowalski case, made a Reel calling out HeyDude for posting with UF Theta Chi, writing in a caption “@heydude what the actual heck is your problem #maddiekowalski.” “HeyDude is sending the same message we're seeing out of Cornell and the DA's office: Survivor experiences [are] unimportant to us,” she tells WIRED. She believes the company “has chosen to reward sexual [exploitation] with a lack of accountability and free PR swag.”
After seeing the collab post with HeyDude, Kowalski tells WIRED she and her mother emailed the company to ask why they had decided to work with the UF chapter. She says they did not hear back.
In a statement to WIRED, a HeyDude spokesperson says the company “has no affiliation, sponsorship, or ongoing partnership” with UF Theta Chi and that the post was part of a larger “HeyDude Tailgate Tour” visiting various locations, including frat and sorority houses, across the country.
“We were unaware of the allegations made against” members of the UF Theta Chi chapter “when the tour was planned,” the spokesperson says. “Our company does not support this alleged behavior and takes allegations such as these very seriously. We will reevaluate future stops for the remainder of the tour.”
As of Friday morning, the post was still up.
Update: 10/2/2026, 5:10 PM EDT: WIRED updated the article clarifying the description of how UF responded to the planned protest.
results.summary:
Footwear brand HeyDude faces public backlash after posting a promotional collaboration with the University of Florida chapter of Theta Chi, a fraternity linked to recent sexual cyberharassment allegations.

### Key Points
- HeyDude, owned by Crocs, featured UF Theta Chi members in social media posts promoting its "Wally" loafers on September 25.
- Two former UF Theta Chi members, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, face criminal charges for allegedly disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a student.
- The victim, Maddie Kowalski, is currently suing the two former members for damages in the Florida Northern District Court.
- HeyDude stated it had no formal partnership with the fraternity and was unaware of the allegations when planning its "HeyDude Tailgate Tour."
- The company is currently reevaluating future tour stops following widespread criticism regarding its association with the fraternity.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing pressure on consumer brands to conduct thorough due diligence when engaging in influencer marketing or campus-based promotional partnerships. It underscores how corporate associations with organizations facing serious misconduct allegations can trigger significant reputational damage and consumer boycotts.

results.title: Where every US governor stands on AI and the data-center boom
results.author: Tristin Hoffman
results.content:
It's up to voters whether artificial intelligence will play a role in the outcome of the coming midterm elections.
The AI boom — and the infrastructure needed to power it — has slowly become a flashpoint in US politics. The debate ranges from AI safety, regulation, and deepfakes to the rapid expansion of data centers.
Many Big Tech firms advocate for faster expansion, while local residents have pushed back against data-center projects over their potential environmental and energy-cost impacts.
One big question for voters: What roles should state and federal governments play in regulating AI? Another is how much power local communities should have over the data centers increasingly being built in their backyards.
Governors across the political spectrum — 17 of whom are up for reelection this year — have taken varied approaches to the AI boom. All 39 gubernatorial races, across 36 states and three territories, are on November 3.
Some governors, including California's Gavin Newsom (D) and New York's Kathy Hochul (D), are exploring an AI "kill switch" that would disable advanced AI systems in an out-of-control event. Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox has also called for federal AI safety rules.
Others, including the Republican governors of Nevada and North Dakota and the Democratic governors of Michigan and New Mexico — whose states have major AI-computing projects under construction — see data centers as an economic opportunity.
Here's what every US governor has said so far about AI, data centers, or both.
Alabama
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has approached AI as an opportunity to improve government, but one that needs guardrails.
In 2024, she created a statewide generative AI task force to examine how it could be used within the state government, emphasizing both the usage of AI and transparency, privacy, and public safety.
"GenAI represents a monumental step forward in the potential for our state government to serve the public," Ivey said in a 2024 statement. "However, its capabilities must first be studied carefully to ensure it is implemented in the most responsible and efficient manner possible."
She is one of the few governors across the US who have taken a harder line on Chinese AI tools. In 2025, Ivey issued a ban on Chinese-affiliated artificial intelligence platforms DeepSeek and Manus from all state-owned devices and networks.
Alaska
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) has pitched the state as a potential hub for the AI boom and the computing infrastructure needed for it, arguing that Alaska has an "arctic advantage."
Dunleavy has said he believes Alaska's colder climate can significantly reduce the cost of cooling AI server racks, saying in late 2025 that an Alaskan 1-gigawatt campus could save operators up to $150 million annually in cooling costs compared to a warmer state.
Dunleavy has also said that data centers could be an economic driver for Alaska, particularly by creating more construction jobs across the state.
He frequently uses AI, too, incorporating certain tools into his work as governor, including using the technology during meetings.
Arizona
Katie Hobbs (D), Arizona's governor up for reelection, has largely framed AI as an economic opportunity that the state needs to prepare for, rather than turn away from.
Hobbs has said she does not support a moratorium, which is a temporary pause, on new data-center development. At the same time, she has pushed for more structure around AI.
Her administration created the state's first AI steering committee in 2025 and launched an AI government tool in 2026, and she has described the goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state's economy.
"Arizona has built one of the strongest AI ecosystems in the country, and our community colleges help power it," Hobbs wrote in a January 22 post on X.
Arkansas
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), who is up for reelection, has said she believes AI has the potential to strengthen government efficiency, but it requires proper policies and regulations.
"AI is changing how we work, interact, and find information — and Arkansas can't afford to be left behind," she wrote in a statement in February following a new state AI effectiveness and safety report.
The report, which was completed by an AI working group that Sanders launched in 2024, found that AI could help the state improve Medicaid and SNAP programs and expand other digital services.
Earlier this year, she also joined RAISE US, a national artificial intelligence initiative launched by former Indiana governor Eric Holcomb and former US Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo. The initiative intends to partner with governors, employers, workers and training organizations to help the workforce transition to an AI economy.
She was one of several politicians who urged Congress to remove the AI regulatory moratorium from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill in 2025.
California
California's Gavin Newsom (D) has moved from a more cautious approach to AI regulation toward some of the most aggressive AI-safety proposals in the country.
After vetoing an AI safety bill in 2024, Newsom has since signed legislation creating independent oversight and auditing requirements on AI systems.
Now, Newsom is backing the idea of an AI "kill switch," which would be an emergency shutoff for frontier AI models, as part of a September executive order. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has proposed a similar idea.
Newsom has also directed experts to consider independent verification of AI companies' safety systems, arguing that California should move ahead even as federal action remains limited.
Colorado
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) signed Senate Bill 24-205 in 2024, making Colorado the first state to enact a comprehensive consumer-protection law aimed at protecting consumers from AI-driven algorithmic discrimination in areas such as employment, housing, education, and healthcare.
That bill was later repealed by Polis this year, however. In his repeal, he narrowed the state's framework by mandating specific transparency, documentation, and consumer rights when automated tools "materially influence" consequential decisions.
The new bill will take effect on January 1, 2027.
Polis has also shown some support for a federal moratorium on state AI laws restricting artificial intelligence, according to a 2025 Bloomberg article.
Connecticut
Ned Lamont (D), governor of Connecticut and up for reelection, signed a bipartisan AI bill earlier this year addressing youth online safety.
Lamont's approach is focused on preparing people to work alongside AI rather than restricting its use. He's also invested in workforce training designed to help Connecticut workers compete for jobs in the tech market: In February, he launched the third phase of the state's Tech Talent Accelerator, a program that aims to expand AI education and workforce training.
Delaware
Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer (D) has sought to make the state a place where companies can experiment with AI without abandoning regulation.
In 2025, he signed legislation launching an AI regulatory sandbox where companies can test AI technologies under government oversight, particularly in corporate governance, health care, biotechnology and financial services.
Meyer has described the sandbox as a way to combine innovation with transparency and public trust.
"This initiative creates space for visionaries and risk-takers to responsibly test cutting-edge artificial intelligence technologies in Delaware—prioritizing transparency, public trust, and thoughtful oversight," he wrote in a statement.
Florida
Ron DeSantis (R), Florida's governor, has pushed for protections around AI rather than banning the technology or leaving it unregulated.
His proposed AI Bill of Rights in late 2025 included data-privacy protections, parental controls, consumer disclosures and restrictions on using someone's name, image or likeness without consent.
"The AI Bill of Rights defends consumers, medical patients, and families in Florida from the potential harms of artificial intelligence applications," he wrote on X in March. "It is especially important that we protect the most vulnerable among us: our children."
Regarding data centers, DeSantis signed a bill earlier this year that would prevent residents from bearing the costs of hyperscale data centers through utility bills and give local governments more authority over where those facilities are built.
Georgia
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) sees AI as an economic opportunity the state cannot afford to ignore.
He has backed the expansion of data centers and has positioned Georgia as a potential hub for the country's AI infrastructure, meeting directly with OpenAI and Georgia Power in July to discuss OpenAI's activity in the state, sites of interest, jobs, and investment commitments.
Much of his approach has focused on building the electricity and infrastructure needed to attract AI investment to the state.
Hawaii
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green (D), up for reelection, has taken a cautious approach to AI.
In July, he signed legislation establishing new safety measures for it — particularly surrounding 'deepfakes', which imitate one's voice and face — saying AI presents "fascinating opportunities" but that the state needs to be intentional about recognizing its potential dangers.
Idaho
Idaho Gov. Brad Little (R), who is up for reelection, has focused heavily on preparing students for an AI-driven economy.
In March, his administration launched a partnership with Microsoft, Micron and other technology companies to teach K-12 students and teachers how to adopt AI into the classroom.
While Micron will teach teachers how to use AI, Microsoft will provide AI literacy programs and its chatbot, Copilot, for all students over 13 and teachers.
Illinois
JB Pritzker, Illinois' governor up for reelection, views artificial intelligence as a transformative tool that also poses severe, existential risks to humanity.
"It's time to sound the alarm — louder — on reining in Artificial Intelligence," Pritzker wrote in an early September statement. "It's becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I'm calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington. When AI researchers are whistleblowing, we need to listen."
His statement urged a stop to Big Tech's lobbying against safety, Congressional hearings on AI safety, and more.
Pritzker also established an AI cabinet in September to assess the various safety risks posed by AI.
Indiana
Mike Braun (R), Indiana's governor, views AI as an economic opportunity to boost wages, create jobs, and to position Indiana as a leader in AI's adoption.
In April, he launched an initiative titled IN AI to help Indiana businesses understand where AI can improve their work, how to access and use different AI tools, and where to find employees across the state who understand the technology.
He has publicly cautioned against building data centers in the state that drain Indiana's water resources.
The state is home to two large data-center projects in the US, however, housing Meta's data center that is expected to deliver 1 gigawatt of capacity and span 1,500 acres in Lebanon, as well as Google's Fort Wayne Data Center, which will require up to 1.2 gigawatts of power at full build-out.
Iowa
In February, Iowa's Gov. Kim Reynolds banned DeepSeek and RedNote, two Chinese-owned apps, from state devices. She also prohibited all state agencies from subscribing to or having an account on either app.
Reynolds has shown a focus on how to responsibly adopt AI, signing an Act in May that regulates AI chatbots, particularly for minors. One of the regulations in the Act provides disclaimers at the beginning of each chat and once every three hours.
Kansas
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly (D) supports a regulated approach to AI that balances the innovation it brings.
In August, Kelly told the Topeka Capital-Journal that there needs to be guardrails around data center construction and the water and energy use associated with them.
In August 2023, she created an AI policy that requires reviews of accuracy, appropriateness, privacy, and security before any action is taken or information is shared.
Kentucky
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) is an advocate for federal oversight and regulation of AI to balance its benefits with risks such as national security and job displacement.
He signed an executive order in August to mitigate the potential environmental and cost impacts of data centers. Specifically, the order requires the companies building the data centers to submit a plan to the state's Energy and Environment Cabinet detailing how they will cover their full energy costs.
Louisiana
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry (R) also views AI as a way to drive economic growth, but said it poses security and utility cost risks.
In June, Landry issued an executive order requiring data centers seeking state sales-tax breaks to protect ratepayers from higher electricity costs, unless the state determines the project's other benefits outweigh the higher electricity costs.
In 2025, Landry, like Iowa's governor, also signed an executive order banning China's DeepSeek across all state agencies.
"As technology advances, so do the threats," he wrote in a statement. "This executive order ensures we are protecting our people, our data, and our national security from the CCP's growing influence in AI."
The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, housing Meta's Hyperion AI data center, a more than $50 billion investment that will span more than 3,600 acres and is planned to deliver 5 gigawatts of capacity once fully developed.
Maine
Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) has taken a more cautious approach toward the growing AI industry.
This year, Mills vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have placed a temporary pause on data center construction requiring 20 or more megawatts of power. She's also said she supported a federal moratorium if it had exempted a specific project that she believed could bring jobs to Maine.
In June 2025, Mills signed a bill that bans companies from using chatbots without clear disclosure. The bill also added AI-generated deepfakes to the state's revenge porn laws.
Maryland
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), who is up for reelection, signed an executive order in early September that relieves locals of the costs of the centers' energy usage, includes environmental protection efforts and AI job training, and establishes a "public dashboard" where locals can express their input on the centers.
Moore's executive order also established the Maryland Data Center Task Force, which will review data center projects, maintain a public data center dashboard, and more.
"My fear is a technology that no human being can control," Moore told MS NOW reporters in late September. "We've got to understand that delicate balance of cooperation and competition. As a governor, I'm very competitive with my other governors. But I do understand that there are places where the focus is cooperation and not competition."
Massachusetts
Maura Healey (D), Massachusetts' governor up for reelection, has argued that AI shouldn't advance faster than the government can protect people from its risks. In September, Healey called for federal action to strengthen AI guardrails and oversight that both allow for innovation and protect national security.
Like Moore, Healey's administration has also created a state AI task force. The state's task force, created in 2024, also includes a $100 million Applied AI Hub that studies how to apply AI to advance Massachusetts' life sciences, healthcare, financial services, advanced manufacturing, robotics, and education sectors.
"AI has enormous potential to drive scientific discovery, strengthen key industries, improve public services, and create new opportunities for businesses and residents across Massachusetts," Gov. Healey wrote in a September press release. "At the same time, the rapid pace of AI development raises serious concerns about safety, accountability, privacy, civil rights, the future of work, and public trust."
Michigan
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) has welcomed data center construction, such as Oracle and OpenAI's project in Saline Township, but with guidelines.
Her July action plan ensures that data center companies pay construction and operation costs, strengthen and safeguard the state's electric grid and natural resources, and are accountable for their development.
"It's simple: any data center company that wants to invest in Michigan must ensure working families do not pay a single penny for data center development or operations, protect our natural resources, and create local, good-paying jobs," Whitmer wrote in a press release.
Michigan is home to The Barn, a $16 billion, 1.4-gigawatt data-center campus in Saline Township that Related Digital is building for Oracle and OpenAI as part of the Stargate project.
Minnesota
Tim Walz (D), Minnesota's governor, signed a law in May prohibiting access to "nudification" technology that can generate fake nude images of real people.
"This bill makes clear that using technology to create fake, non-consensual intimate images is unacceptable and puts Minnesota at the forefront of addressing the harms of AI while protecting people from exploitation and abuse," Walz wrote in a press release.
The law echoes Walz's broader approach to AI, which encourages its development while drawing lines around any usage that threatens privacy or safety, specifically for children.
In May 2023, he also signed a state law that regulates and restricts the use of deepfakes in political campaigns.
Mississippi
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves (R) signed a memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA in June 2025 to promote AI education, workforce integration, and research collaboration.
His focus is on ensuring Mississippi's workforce can use AI effectively; in May, he launched a statewide AI framework that centers on equipping students and workers with skills in ethical reasoning and AI-related cybersecurity awareness.
During a Sept. 30 Federalist Society conversation, Reeves emphasized that Mississippi works efficiently at cutting deals with companies, particularly AI and data center companies, highlighting the state's $20 billion partnership with xAI was expected to launch only a few weeks after making the deal.
"So many states around the country start at no and give you the burden to ultimately get to yes…" Reeves said. "…We start at yes, and as we navigate our way through it, we've got very seasoned, talented people who run our economic development shop."
Missouri
In May, Mike Kehoe (R), Missouri's governor, announced that Google will invest $15 billion into data center construction in New Florence, a rural town in central Missouri.
Kehoe also signed an executive order in January that allows for growth in data centers and Missouri's use in AI, while calling on economic and natural resources directors to study how AI could impact the local workforce and citizens' energy bills.
The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, Nebius' AI Factory, which will reach a capacity of up to 1.2 gigawatts.
Montana
Greg Gianforte (R), Montana's governor and a former software entrepreneur who founded RightNow Technologies, later acquired by Oracle, has approached AI from a business perspective.
In 2025, he signed Montana's Right to Compute Act, which established legal protections for businesses' use of AI, limiting the government's interference in their use. He also launched 406 JOBS in 2025, a workforce program aimed at modernizing the state's workforce.
Nebraska
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen (R), up for reelection, like several other governors, has expressed that locals shouldn't front the bill for energy costs stemming from data centers.
In July, Pillen ended access to certain state tax incentives for data centers and created a task force to examine their impact on water, electricity, and local infrastructure.
"Early in my administration, I called for a pause in building new data centers, and this executive order is consistent with that call," Pillen wrote in a press release. "Data centers are a booming industry. Major tech companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into them. And while that presents significant economic opportunity, it also presents resource challenges."
Nevada
Joe Lombardo (R), Nevada's governor up for reelection, has emphasized the economic opportunity AI data centers bring for the state.
In September, he signed an executive order requiring data center developers to cover project-related energy costs. The order also aims to support public schools and protect the state's water resources.
Lombardo has said he supports data centers because they bring jobs, investment, and economic growth to the state.
"At the same time, we have to put the right parameters in place to ensure they don't raise costs on Nevada residents or businesses," he wrote in a May Facebook post. "As Governor, I'm focused on growing our economy responsibly while protecting rates for families."
New Hampshire
New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R), who is up for reelection, has shown skepticism toward data centers due to the amount of energy they require.
In August, Ayotte said she supported a moratorium on data centers, arguing that New Hampshire does not have enough energy capacity to support them without hiking up electricity costs. She also said she is opposed to a potential data center being built in Bow, a small town in central New Hampshire.
New Jersey
In September, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) issued a $1.07 million fine to the DataOne data center in Vineland, holding that the data center violated the New Jersey Air Pollution Control Act by installing and operating 62 large natural-gas power generators without Department of Environmental Protection permits.
"Data centers will pay their fair share for energy, be accountable for their water and energy use, protect our environment, create good-paying union jobs, and invest in communities," Sherrill wrote on a social media post.
She has signed legislation requiring data centers to report their electricity and water consumption to the Board of Public Utilities every six months, and also has expressed that AI instruction should be embedded into New Jersey's education programs.
New Mexico
In 2025, Michelle Lujan Grisham (D), New Mexico's governor, announced a $1 billion partnership with Meta on a new geothermal plant for the company's data center. Geothermal energy, which is considered a green power source, taps heat beneath Earth's surface to generate electricity; it can also be used directly for heating and cooling.
The $1 billion investment will create 3,000 construction jobs and 100 jobs running the geothermal power plant. New Mexico touts 22 data centers — one of which is Project Jupiter, one of the largest in the US.
The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, Stargate's Project Jupiter, which could include up to 2.45 gigawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells, replacing an earlier proposal centered on gas turbines and diesel generators.
New York
Kathy Hochul (D), New York's governor up for reelection, like California Gov. Gavin Newsom, is exploring an AI "kill switch" that would shut off AI systems in a critical event.
In late December 2025, she signed the RAISE Act, which requires AI developers to create and publish information about their safety protocols and to report incidents to the state government within 72 hours of an incident.
Under the law, New York's Attorney General can bring civil actions against developers who fail to submit reports, with penalties rising up to $1 million for the first violation and up to $3 million for subsequent violations.
Hochul also issued an executive order imposing a one-year moratorium on large-scale AI data centers in July to evaluate and address their environmental and community impact.
North Carolina
North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein (D), like many governors, has approached AI as both an economic opportunity and a policy challenge.
His administration's AI Strategic Roadmap, launched in July, aims to protect locals from any harm AI might cause, prepare workers for AI-related changes, and use AI to improve government work.
In a speech announcing the roadmap, Stein said AI can help with government efficiency, such as scanning outdated documents and answering residents' questions, but also emphasized the need to address the risks that come with its usage.
North Dakota
Kelly Armstrong (R), North Dakota's governor, signed legislation in 2025 that limits the role of AI in certain health-care decisions, requiring licensed physicians, rather than algorithms, to make final decisions in some cases.
Armstrong also sees AI as an economic opportunity, holding that North Dakota's natural-gas industry could help supply the energy data centers need.
Similar to Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Armstrong believes the state's colder climate can allow AI and data center companies to lower their cooling costs.
Ohio
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said in September that the federal government should enact regulations on AI, not the states.
"Look, as far as AI, this really needs to come from the federal government," DeWine said at an event in New Albany, near Columbus. "We need to have uniformity, not just in this country; we need to have uniformity in the world. So, I would certainly hope we can see some uniformity coming out of Washington."
In May, he also paused new applications for data center tax exemptions amid growing scrutiny of the state's incentives and the costs associated with large facilities.
According to the governor, in 2025, data centers that had been granted sales and use tax benefits in the state reported a total capital investment of $27.2 billion.
The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, housing Nvidia-backed project PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, which is expected to include up to 10 gigawatts of data-center capacity.
Oklahoma
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) created an AI task force in 2023 to study how the technology could improve government efficiency, education, and workforce development, and has repeatedly described Oklahoma as a potential AI hub.
Stitt's task force was completed in 2024 and recommended five ways the state can implement AI into its workforce and government, largely by creating oversight, economic, digital, and talent workforce committees that encourage the use of AI across sectors.
"Oklahoma is poised to lead the nation in implementation of artificial intelligence technology, and we have to capitalize on the momentum. Oklahoma truly could be the AI capital of the nation," Stitt wrote in a 2024 press release.
Like other governors, he aims to protect ratepayers from increasing energy costs related to data centers, but also has stated that he supports the construction of data centers, highlighting property rights and the free market.
Oregon
Oregon's Tina Kotek (D), who is up for reelection, has said states cannot wait for federal action on AI.
In September, Kotek issued an executive order similar to those of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, directing the state to assess the viability of a "kill switch" requirement for frontier AI models.
"It's encouraging to hear AI companies are beginning to come forward with proposals to address safety concerns, but we cannot simply wait for the private sector to self-regulate a technology that poses such an existential and evolving risk," Kotek wrote in a press release.
Pennsylvania
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), up for reelection, said at a September AI Horizons Summit that he sees AI's potential to improve productivity and public services, but argued that the technology needs stronger guardrails.
"I want to be clear: I am not a doomer," he said at the summit. "I don't think it is inevitable that AI is going to take over the world or that someone will misuse it to kill us or do harm."
He also cracked down on data centers in August, saying that data center proposals are scaring and changing the character of Pennsylvania communities.
Rhode Island
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee (D) created an AI task force and Center of Excellence for AI and Data in 2024, both in an effort to study how AI could increase government efficiency and improve public services.
"Rhode Island recognizes that the rise of AI technology will enhance future government operations and change the way we do business," McKee wrote in a press release. "Rather than simply react to the changes in the information technology landscape, I want Rhode Island to be a leader as this field evolves."
South Carolina
Beginning in early 2024, Henry McMaster (R), South Carolina's governor, was the chair of the Southern Regional Education Board Commission on Artificial Intelligence in Education.
In his role, McMaster convened with other education and business leaders to chart a course for the use of AI in classrooms and to prepare the workforce for the technology.
"When used correctly, AI is a powerful tool capable of reshaping our education system," McMaster wrote. "By working together, we can overcome the challenges that AI presents and harness its power to ensure our students are prepared for the workforce of the future."
In general, McMaster is cautious toward rushing into government regulation on AI, arguing that politicians do not have a complete understanding yet of its benefits and drawbacks.
Regarding his view on data centers, McMaster said in late September that he does not plan to call for a statewide data center moratorium.
The state houses three of Google's data centers, which opened in 2007. In 2024, the company announced it would establish two new data center campuses in the state, a combined investment of $3.3 billion.
"Google's latest investment will strengthen South Carolina's position as an emerging leader in technology and innovation," McMaster wrote in a statement.
South Dakota
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden (R), who is up for reelection, has also banned Chinese apps from state devices.
In 2025, Rhoden signed a bill making it a Class 1 misdemeanor to disseminate an undisclosed deepfake intended to injure a candidate within 90 days of an election, punishable by up to a year in jail, a $2,000 fine, or both.
He is one of several governors who signed a bill that protects residents from increased utility costs caused by data centers.
Tennessee
Bill Lee (R), Tennessee's governor, signed the ELVIS Act — Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act — in 2024 to protect musicians from being cloned or replicated by AI without consent.
Tennessee was the first state in the US to legally protect artists and musicians from deepfakes. Lee also signed a bill earlier this year that prohibits AI developers from falsely posing as qualified mental health professionals.
The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, xAI's Colossus 2, which powers Grok, the AI chatbot on X, and is expected to deliver 1.5 gigawatts in capacity.
Texas
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), up for reelection, has shifted his views toward AI over the past year.
Less than a year ago, Abbott welcomed the plethora of Big Tech companies constructing data centers across the state, calling Texas the "epicenter of AI development."
But with growing backlash toward the uptick in electric and water costs for locals, Abbott has shifted his perspective on data centers, saying that the companies building them "dug their own grave" by failing to also build community support.
In August, Abbott announced that OpenAI would comply with his established data center guidelines, including not passing on costs to Texans or interfering with their quality of life.
The state houses several of the US' largest planned data centers, including Meta's El Paso data center and Fermi America's Project Matador, the latter pursuing up to 17 gigawatts of private power.
Utah
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox (R) called on Congress in September to establish guidelines on AI, including mandatory reporting of major safety incidents, whistleblower protections for tech employees, independent safety evaluations for models, and restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to China.
"We can build the world's most advanced AI here in America while ensuring it remains firmly in service of humanity," Cox wrote on X.
In May, he issued an order establishing a "higher bar" for future data center projects following public backlash against his support for a project near Salt Lake City. The order requires greater transparency and protections for water, air quality, the Great Salt Lake, local communities, and utility customers.
Vermont
Vermont Gov. Phil Scott (R), who is up for reelection, is one of many governors who established a task force to assess how AI might shape the state's economy.
In June, Scott's administration partnered with Anthropic through Vermont's Agency of Digital Services to test state IT systems for security vulnerabilities. The agreement gives the state $100,000 in credits for Claude Code, Anthropic's AI tool.
He also signed legislation requiring disclosure of deceptive and fraudelent AI-generated content used in election campaigns within 90 days of an election.
Virginia
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger is one of several governors who believe states should lead on AI risk assessments rather than wait for Washington to act.
"The federal government needs to play a much larger role in regulating this emerging technology to ensure its safe development and the protection of people and their livelihoods," Spanberger wrote in September.
She created a state AI Task Force in September to examine workforce displacement, data privacy, cybersecurity, and ways existing laws can address AI-related harms.
Regarding data centers, Virginia has the largest data market in the US with over 100,000 jobs and over $40 billion in investments, according to the Northern Virginia Technology Council.
Spanberger recently unveiled a Data Center Accountability Framework, requiring centers to pay their own transmission costs, strengthen environmental and water-use protections, and give communities more input on proposed developments.
Washington
Bob Ferguson (D), Washington's governor, has expressed concern over children's safety when using AI.
Earlier this year, he signed legislation that requires disclosures that people are interacting with AI, safeguards around self-harm content, and protections for minors from sexually explicit conversations.
Ferguson also signed a bill that requires covered AI providers to include provenance data in AI-generated or materially altered images, video, and audio.
West Virginia
West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey (R) has said he views the state as a "powerhouse" for AI and cloud computing, announcing earlier this year that Penzance Management will invest $4 billion in an AI campus in Berkeley County, about 75 miles northwest of Washington, DC.
"By earning the state's first High Impact Intelligence Center designation, Penzance is helping us transform the Mountain State into a powerhouse for artificial intelligence and cloud computing," he wrote in a statement. "This project brings a massive new revenue stream to our communities - all driven by private capital and our commitment to a business-friendly, reliable energy strategy."
Morrisey has also supported AI health tools that reduce administrative work for rural providers.
Wisconsin
Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D) has focused his approach toward AI on how it affects the workforce.
In 2023, he created the Governor's Task Force on Workforce and Artificial Intelligence to assess how the technology could reshape Wisconsin jobs, skills, and key industries. Its 2024 action plan focused on preparing workers and institutions for an AI-driven economy.
He has also welcomed data center projects, saying they can be built while still protecting the environment and the local communities.
Wyoming
Mark Gordon (R), Wyoming's governor, sees AI as an opportunity to grow the state's economy, especially through data centers and advanced computing.
Earlier this year, he issued "Data Centers the Wyoming Way," an executive order intended to create a statewide framework for data-center development, including its energy, water, and community impacts.
"While other states hit the pause button out of political fear, we are choosing action and collaboration," Gov. Gordon wrote in a statement to Business Insider. "We are proving America's digital infrastructure can be built the Wyoming Way."
results.summary:
US governors are increasingly shaping the national AI landscape through diverse policies, ranging from aggressive safety regulations and "kill switch" proposals to aggressive economic incentives for data-center infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Governors in states like California, New York, and Oregon are exploring "kill switch" mechanisms to disable advanced AI systems during critical safety failures.
- Many states, including Texas, Michigan, and Maryland, have implemented frameworks requiring data-center developers to cover their own energy and infrastructure costs to protect local ratepayers.
- Several governors, such as those in Alaska, North Dakota, and Wyoming, are actively courting AI investment by highlighting their states' cold climates for cooling efficiency and business-friendly policies.
- Legislative actions across the country include bans on Chinese-affiliated AI platforms, protections against deepfakes in elections, and the establishment of state-level AI task forces.
- Tennessee became the first state to pass legislation protecting artists and musicians from unauthorized AI voice and likeness cloning via the ELVIS Act.

### Why it Matters
The fragmented state-level response to AI and data-center expansion creates a complex regulatory patchwork that forces tech companies to navigate varying compliance standards across the US. As governors balance the promise of economic growth against concerns over energy consumption and public safety, their individual policies are effectively serving as a testing ground for future federal oversight.

results.content:
Job growth in the United States slowed in September, falling short of economists’ expectations as the unemployment rate rose in the final jobs report before the consequential midterm elections.
The US economy added 29,000 jobs in September, according to the Labor Department’s report released on Friday, far below economists’ expectations. Dow Jones had forecast 84,000 jobs, while economists polled by Reuters said they expected 90,000 job additions.
The unemployment rate also rose by 0.1 percentage point, from 4.1 percent to 4.2 percent.
The healthcare sector led the gains, accounting for the majority of new jobs. The industry added 17,000 jobs, marking a slowdown from an average of 33,000 jobs per month over the past year. Construction added 11,000 jobs, while manufacturing added 9,000.
Financial activities, which include sectors such as commercial banking and insurance, shed 7,000 jobs.
Most other sectors were largely unchanged, including retail, oil and gas extraction, and leisure and hospitality.
“Today’s disappointing report shows the labour market is grinding to a halt, marked by slow hiring and declining real wages that leave workers with very little leverage,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at the think tank The Century Foundation, said in remarks provided to Al Jazeera.
Previous jobs reports were also revised downward. July was revised from an initial gain of 21,000 jobs to a loss of 10,000 jobs. August was revised down by 29,000 jobs, from 162,000 to 133,000.
Wages grew by 3 percent, marking the slowest annual wage increase in five years.
Friday’s jobs report caps a week of weakening economic data before the consequential midterm election on November 3.
According to an AP-NORC poll released on Thursday, 61 percent of Americans polled said the US economy is worse off now than when Trump took office in January 2025.
“When businesses are barely hiring and raises aren’t keeping up with rising prices, it’s a stalled economy – and working families are stuck in it,” Breyon Williams, chief economist for Groundwork Collaborative, an economic policy think tank, said in a statement.
Trump has been trying to change the narrative on the slumping economy. On Monday, he said in a Truth Social post that “The United States has the BEST Employment Numbers in HISTORY.”
Stalling growth
On Tuesday, the US Labor Department released the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, or JOLTS report, which showed little change, suggesting what economists call a low-hire, low-fire environment. That means those who have jobs are generally not leaving for new ones, while employers are maintaining the status quo rather than expanding.
On the other hand, ADP’s private payroll report, released on Wednesday, showed that 90,000 jobs were created across the private sector. The sheer number of layoffs fell, too, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The report, released Thursday, showed that employers cut more than 43,000 jobs in September, marking an 18 percent decline in layoffs from August.
Friday’s jobs report comes before the Federal Reserve’s final policy decision before the midterm election. During its two-day policy meeting on October 27-28, the central bank will decide whether to raise, cut or maintain interest rates.
The odds increasingly suggest the Fed will hold rates steady in the 3.75-4.00 percent range, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions. The FedWatch tool indicates there is currently a 77.3 percent chance that rates will hold steady, up from 35.8 percent this time last week.
US markets are trending upward on the heels of the report. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is up 1.5 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 0.6 percent and the S&P 500 is up 1.1 percent in midday trading.
The price of gold, which is largely considered a safe investment during times of economic uncertainty, rose 1.1 percent to $4,223.49 amid the jobs report.
results.summary:
The United States labor market experienced a significant slowdown in September as job growth fell short of expectations and the national unemployment rate increased to 4.2 percent.

### Key Points
- The U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs in September, significantly missing analyst forecasts of 84,000 to 90,000 new positions.
- The national unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage point to reach 4.2 percent.
- Healthcare led sector gains with 17,000 new jobs, while the financial activities sector shed 7,000 positions.
- Annual wage growth slowed to 3 percent, representing the lowest increase recorded in five years.
- Previous job growth figures for July and August were revised downward by the Labor Department.
- Market reactions included a rise in major stock indices and a 1.1 percent increase in the price of gold.

### Why it Matters
This report signals a cooling labor market just days before the November 3 midterm elections, intensifying political debates regarding the current state of the economy. The data also influences expectations for the Federal Reserve, which is now widely anticipated to maintain current interest rates during its upcoming policy meeting.
